claims.text: An active-learning MLIP trained on a limited set of ab initio configurations near fusion conditions can reproduce the free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid phases.
The MLIP can retain vibrational-entropy and anharmonic contributions to the phase free energies.
The MLIP can retain electron–vibration coupling effects.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy workflows.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
Free-energy predictions from the MLIP workflow will remain within approximately 5% of fully converged ab initio results.
Melting temperatures obtained from solid–liquid free-energy crossings will closely match established benchmarks.
Active learning selectively adds ab initio training data in regions of configuration space that are important for accurate free energies.
A modest number of ab initio energy and force evaluations is sufficient to capture the thermodynamic contributions needed for fusion calculations.
Using the trained MLIP permits rapid phase-space sampling and free-energy integration.
The workflow is expected to perform robustly for elemental systems.
The workflow is expected to perform robustly for binary systems.
The workflow can be extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys when additional training data sufficiently cover their configurational space.
Extremely complex configurational spaces may limit MLIP performance, particularly where electron–vibration coupling is difficult to represent.
Prior MLIP successes in similar fusion or high-temperature thermodynamic contexts support the proposed approach.
The proposed intervention is to iteratively refine an MLIP using ab initio energies and forces from short molecular-dynamics trajectories at fusion conditions and then apply free-energy integration.
The workflow is rejected if free energies or melting temperatures differ from ab initio baselines by more than approximately 5%, or if melting temperature differs by more than 50 K.
The workflow is also rejected if it fails to provide an order-of-magnitude computational-cost improvement.
